clue.text: Their eldest hope, their Jenny, (Robert Burns)

definitions.text: Their eldest hope, their Jenny, (Robert Burns)

parts.words: Their eldest hope, their Jenny, (Robert Burns)
parts.note: a line from Burns's poem The Cotter's Saturday Night with its last two words missing, describing the cottager's grown-up daughter

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: the solver completes the Burns line, which describes the eldest daughter coming home as an adult.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns's line calls the daughter Jenny fully adult, which is the sense of the missing compound.

clue.text: Sensational successes, starting with old Wordsworth sonnets

indicators.note: starting points of the four words from 'with' onward are taken, one letter from each word in turn

explanation.surface: A survey of big literary hits begins with the early sonnets of William Wordsworth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' looks like a link word but is the first of the four words whose initials are taken by 'starting'.
explanation.definitionFit: Huge hits that amaze an audience are informally called this, a plural noun from an exclamation of delight.

clue.text: Eliot's eponymous disaster scene

parts.note: George Eliot named a novel after the riverside building where its closing flood disaster strikes, the one on the Floss

explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot's novel takes its title from the Tullivers' watermill, the setting of its fatal flood.

clue.text: Revised will found in old book?

parts.note: a revised version is a new one
a will is a person's last testament

explanation.surface: Someone's updated will turns up inside an antique volume.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the joke: this 'new' book of the Bible is nearly two thousand years old.
explanation.definitionFit: The second part of the Christian Bible is an ancient scripture, so old despite its name.

clue.text: Member of religion from former era stays loyal to emperor

indicators.note: the answer is taken out of the run of letters across these words, so it comes from them

explanation.surface: A believer from an earlier age remains faithful to an emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loyal to emperor' adds colour to the definition: the faith reveres the Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie.
explanation.definitionFit: A Rastafarian, follower of a Jamaican faith revering Haile Selassie, is known by this short form.

clue.text: Violated Sabine wed in German city

indicators.note: violated suggests something broken or abused, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Sabine woman is forcibly married in a German town, echoing the Roman legend.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the rape of the Sabine women; 'Violated' rearranges SABINE and WED.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hessian spa town on the Rhine is the state capital of Hesse.

clue.text: Ward took one to Berlin

parts.note: the satirist Ned Ward titled his travel pieces in the pattern 'A ... to' a place, a single stride of a journey

explanation.definitionFit: A single pace taken toward a destination is the unit in Ward's travel titles.

clue.text: Ethical art? could be dramatically so

definitions.note: an adverb phrase for an adjective: the answer describes something done dramatically

indicators.note: could be signals that the letters of the phrase might become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Morally upright art may turn out to be a bit of a show.
explanation.definitionFit: Something staged and showy behaves as if on a stage, in an exaggerated way.

clue.text: Greek robber shows impertinence in bad prose

indicators.note: in places the cheeky word within the scrambled letters of the other
bad prose is poorly made, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: crust is old slang for cheek or impertinence

explanation.surface: A Greek bandit reveals his cheek in clumsy writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges the letters of the clue's second noun, and 'in' sets the slang for cheek inside them; 'shows' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical bandit of Attica stretched or cut his victims to fit his bed.

clue.text: Benevolent character of Lucie-Smith

parts.note: a kindly figure, also the title of a poem by Edward Lucie-Smith

explanation.definitionFit: A person who hopes for others' good fortune is a benevolent figure.

clue.text: Joyce's posthumous leading man takes a 6 with a bird

definitions.text: Joyce's posthumous leading man takes a 6 with a bird

parts.words: Joyce's posthumous leading man takes a 6 with a bird
parts.note: Joyce's novel published after his death is named for its lead, Stephen, which splits as 6-across plus a female bird; the light is the remaining word of the title

explanation.walkthrough: The 6 is 6-across: that word plus HEN (a bird) spells STEPHEN, first word of Joyce's Stephen ___.
explanation.definitionFit: A leading man is the protagonist, and Joyce's early draft novel names him so in its title.

clue.text: Required ancient history authority. Job description included

definitions.text: Required ancient history authority. Job description included

parts.words: Required ancient history authority. Job description included
parts.note: the earlier part of the Bible is a revered source on early history and contains the Book of Job

explanation.walkthrough: 'Job description' looks like an office term; it is the Book of Job.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebrew scriptures are the first part of the Christian Bible, containing the Book of Job.

clue.text: Up to a Rambler new edition, to reveal early means of transport

indicators.note: a new edition reissues the same material reworked, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fresh printing of Johnson's periodical The Rambler shows an old form of travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reveal' is a link; 'new edition' rearranges UP TO A RAMBLER.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby carriage, the pram, is a means of carrying a child in its earliest years.

clue.text: "A newspaper was thought too refined and " (Charles Lamb, Essays of Elia)

definitions.text: "A newspaper was thought too refined and " (Charles Lamb, Essays of Elia)

parts.words: "A newspaper was thought too refined and " (Charles Lamb, Essays of Elia)
parts.note: a sentence from Lamb's Elia essays with its final word missing, describing a paper as too lofty

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: complete Lamb's sentence with the word meaning remote or theoretical.
explanation.definitionFit: Paired with 'refined', the missing word means remote from everyday matters, theoretical.

clue.text: The French among Scotch flowers inclined to fight for no good reason

definitions.text: inclined to fight for no good reason
definitions.note: an adjective phrase for a noun: the answer is the person so inclined

indicators.note: among places the French article between the two river names

parts.note: flowers are rivers here, and the Tweed and the Dee are rivers of Scotland
le is French for the

explanation.surface: French visitors among Scottish blooms are spoiling for a pointless scrap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowers' means things that flow, so rivers, not blooms; the Tweed and the Dee are both Scottish rivers. The definition alludes to Lewis Carroll's quarrelsome brothers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lewis Carroll, the two brothers agree to battle over a spoilt rattle, a quarrel without cause.

clue.text: Sort of elementary observation?

parts.note: Conan Doyle's detective's deductions are famed as 'elementary', so this is the kind of observation he makes

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes deduction in the manner of Conan Doyle's Baker Street detective.

clue.text: Sign of early Romans

parts.note: the zodiac sign Gemini shows a pair born together, as were Romulus and Remus, founders of Rome

explanation.definitionFit: Gemini is the zodiac sign of a pair of brothers, and Rome's founders were such a pair.

clue.text: Somerville and Ross's central character (not Irish) produces heat

indicators.note: not Irish tells us to remove that word from the character's title

parts.note: the hero of Somerville and Ross's stories is the Irish Resident Magistrate, known as the Irish R.M.

explanation.surface: Two Irish authors' hero, minus his nationality, generates warmth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'produces' is a link; 'not' strips IRISH out of THE IRISH RM.
explanation.definitionFit: A therm is a unit of heat energy used in billing for gas.

clue.text: Pinter's view with quiet association

parts.note: a scenic view, and the title of a quiet two-voice play by Harold Pinter

explanation.definitionFit: A wide view of countryside is a scenic vista, and Pinter's short play bears this title.

clue.text: Total article to be right memory for Scott's laird

parts.note: a total is all of something
an is the indefinite article
the infinitive to be gives the word be
RAM is computer memory

explanation.surface: An accounting of every item including a recollection, made for a Scottish landowner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Laird of Ellangowan in Scott's novel Guy Mannering bears this name.

clue.text: Her smiles are welcome though she can be tetchy

definitions.text: Her smiles are welcome though she can be tetchy

parts.words: Her smiles are welcome though she can be tetchy
parts.note: the Greek goddess of fortune is welcome when she favours you but capricious, her name near in letters to tetchy

explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of chance and luck brings fortune good or bad.

clue.text: Quest of Dean Koontz

parts.note: in Waugh's A Handful of Dust, Tony Last is held in the Amazon by a man who makes him read Dickens aloud

clue.text: School for dictionary researcher's biographer

definitions.meaning: a famous English public school in Hampshire
Simon ... wrote the life of W. C. Minor, a contributor to the Oxford English Dictionary, in The Surgeon of Crowthorne

explanation.surface: A school is chosen for the biographer of a dictionary helper.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hampshire public school shares its name with the author of The Professor and the Madman.

clue.text: The profound work of Benchley

Peter Benchley's novel The ... followed Jaws
